name: Gareth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Gareth. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. To begin, what's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Valleyfresh superstore on the retail park, the big one next to the carpet place. Most days I run the bank of fourteen self-checkouts, so I'm the one fixing 'unexpected item in bagging area' fifty times a shift, and I cover a till when the queue backs up. In the afternoon I pick click-and-collect orders with a handheld scanner. What I like is when a machine jams and I get to open it up before the engineer comes; what wears me down is the same three complaints all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a studio flat above the bookies on Station Road, on my own. I've got about two weeks of money saved and six hundred on a credit card I'm slowly paying off. Valleyfresh is the only big shop round here, so if it went, I'd be on two buses to the city for the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overdone, but the useful bits are still useful. I'd post that I use AI every day for little stuff, like working out my budget or explaining a wiring diagram. At work I'd tell people not to relax too much, because Valleyfresh still wants to cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't save me. I'm on lower pay for this job and there's nowhere else to go locally. I don't want to be running self-checkouts at forty, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI to study for the basic electrics course at the college, which I want to start in January. I'd keep asking Raj, the engineer who services our self-checkouts, if his company takes trainees. And I'd clear that six hundred on the card by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, more than worried. I'd feel like the world said stay put, and I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Raj might take trainees. How did that come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He comes every other Tuesday when a scanner dies, and I always make him a tea and ask what he's doing. Last month he said his firm can't find people who don't mind odd hours. I've got his number now, which is more than most people on the shop floor have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would hold you back from the course in January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly, the fee's about three hundred and I haven't got it spare. I'd ask about paying in bits, or ask the union whether there's a learning fund. If not, I'd wait a term and save, which I'd hate.

say: The hype was overdone, but **daily AI tools** are still genuinely useful.
Staff shouldn't relax, because Valleyfresh still wants to **cut costs**.
think: A quiet AI world doesn't fix his **low pay** or the lack of local jobs.
He doesn't want to run **self-checkouts** at forty, whatever happens.
do: **Study** for the January **electrics course** with AI help.
**Ask** Raj, the self-checkout engineer, whether his firm takes **trainees**.
**Clear** the **£600** credit card debt by summer.
feel: **Restless** rather than worried, wanting to move when the world says **stay put**.
S0.quote: I don't want to be running self-checkouts at forty, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: His drive comes from **ambition**, not fear of AI.
He has quietly built a **contact**: the engineer Raj, over cups of tea.
The **£300 course fee** is the real barrier, which shows how thin his cushion is.

steps.text: Start the basic electrics evening course at the college in January
Ask Raj's servicing firm about trainee engineer places
Pay off the £600 credit card by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance if we're smart about it, and a disaster if we let the company decide everything. I'd push the union to ask for training money as part of any deal. Online I'd post the stuff I'm learning, so others on the shop floor can see it's not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tills shrink and the machines grow, so I want to be the one fixing the machines. The ordering, the rota and the customer emails go to software first, and that's not my job anyway. The hands-on side, jams and broken scanners, sticks around longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrics course and then ask Valleyfresh if they'd let me shadow Raj on his visits. I'd use AI every night to learn fault codes for our self-checkout model. I'd also cut my phone contract down to the cheap one so I can pay the course fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick at the same time. I know where I want to go, but the floor might move before I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the floor might move. What does that look like at Valleyfresh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They drop from six people on tills to two, and click-and-collect gets done by a picking robot in the back. If my hours go before I've got the electrics ticket, I can't pay the studio. That's the gap that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev on the fish counter, she's been there twenty years and won't touch an app. And the Saturday kids, who'll never get the first job I got. I'd want the union to fight for both of them, not just for people like me who'll be fine.

say: This is a **chance** if workers have a say, a **disaster** if the company decides alone.
The union should demand **training money** in any deal.
think: Tills will shrink and machines grow, so he wants to **fix the machines**.
Thinking tasks like **ordering** and rotas go to software first, not his job.
do: **Finish** the electrics course and ask to **shadow Raj** on visits.
**Learn** self-checkout **fault codes** with AI every night.
**Switch** to a cheaper **phone contract** to cover the course fee.
feel: **Excited** and slightly sick, fearing the **floor moves** before he arrives.
S1.quote: If my hours go before I've got the electrics ticket, I can't pay the studio.
fieldNote: He has a **clear target**: servicing the machines that replace tills.
His fear is **timing**: hours cut before his new skill pays.
He worries for **Bev** and the Saturday kids more than for himself.

steps.text: Finish the electrics course and shadow Raj on service visits
Learn the self-checkout fault codes with an AI tutor every night
Switch to the cheapest phone contract to fund the course
Push the union to win training money for Bev and others

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need emergency help, a basic income and free training, starting now. Two years is nothing for a family with no savings. I'd organise a meeting in the staff room, even if management hated it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the thinking AI in 2028 hits head office, not me, and the robots in 2031 hit me. My plan to fix machines still works for a while, but in a world where robots are as good as people, they'll fix each other eventually. So I've got maybe five years of a good trade, not forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a fast-track electrics course, even if it means borrowing from my dad. I'd try to get hired by a robot servicing firm before 2031, when everyone else will want the same job. And I'd use AI every day to learn the robot side, not just the wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'm the adaptable one and even I can see the window shutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd borrow from your dad. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, he's a postman and he's got his own worries. But I'd rather owe him for a course than owe a bank for rent. I'd pay him back in the first year of the new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the whole game for me. In 2028 my till job is still safe because a person still has to lift and fix things. Those three years are my chance to get into the servicing side before everyone else panics.

say: Two years is nothing, so people need **basic income** and **free training** now.
Staff should **organise** in the staff room, whatever management thinks.
think: Thinking AI hits **head office** in 2028, but robots reach him in **2031**.
Fixing robots may give him **five good years**, not a whole career.
do: **Borrow** from his dad for a **fast-track** electrics course.
**Study** the **robot side**, not just the wiring, with AI every day.
feel: **Alarmed**, because even the adaptable one can see the **window shutting**.
S2.quote: I'm the adaptable one and even I can see the window shutting.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** as a deliberate launch window.
He doubts a repair trade survives once **robots fix robots**.
Borrowing from his **postman dad** shows how thin the cushion is.

steps.text: Take a fast-track electrics course in the first six months
Borrow the course fee from his dad and repay within a year
Apply to robot servicing firms before 2031
Study robot maintenance with AI tools every evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if the government stops dithering and pays for courses. I'd post my own plan online, step by step, so other shop workers can copy it. And I'd keep pushing the union for a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. I can do the electrics course, get a year with Raj's firm, and be properly trained before AGI in 2031. The robots come for the shop floor around 2034, and by then I want to be the bloke who installs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the electrics course and pay for it myself by cutting back. Then I'd apply for an apprenticeship with a servicing firm. I'd keep my weekend shifts at Valleyfresh so I've still got rent coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually, with a bit of nerves. It's fast but it's a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction between wanting to install the robots and backing the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't think so. The robots are coming whether I install them or not. I'd rather be paid well to do it and still fight for Bev to get a pension and a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the studio, it's cheap for what it is. If the apprenticeship is in the city I'd move there, because two buses each way would kill me. I'd find a room share first and see.

say: Five years is enough if government **pays for courses** instead of dithering.
He'd post his **step-by-step plan** so others on the shop floor can copy it.
think: Five years suits him: course, a year with **Raj's firm**, then trained by 2031.
He wants to be the person who **installs the robots** by 2034.
do: **Pay** for the electrics course by **cutting back** this year.
**Apply** for a servicing **apprenticeship** in year two.
**Keep** weekend Valleyfresh shifts for **rent** during training.
feel: Mostly **good**, with **nerves**, like a race he knows he can run.
S3.quote: The robots are coming whether I install them or not.
fieldNote: He resolves the **union versus robots** tension calmly and practically.
Five years turns alarm into a **workable plan** for him.
Still anxious, because **thin savings** leave no room for a setback.

steps.text: Pay for the electrics course by cutting back this year
Apply for a robot servicing apprenticeship in the second year
Keep weekend Valleyfresh shifts to cover the studio rent
Move into a city room share if the apprenticeship is there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind. Free courses, proper pay for apprentices, and a say for workers in how the robots are used. I'd keep saying it at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel pretty safe. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots reach the shop floor in 2039, and I'll have been an engineer for years by then. The bigger risk is getting comfortable on the tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do the electrics course, no rush, one evening a week. Next year I'd go for a proper apprenticeship and maybe a qualification in robotics later. I'd save a bit each month too, because for once there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the first picture where I feel like I'm the one deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is getting comfortable. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline and tell people. My hard date is off the tills by thirty, and I'd tell my mum so she nags me every Sunday. I do better when someone's checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else do you think about in a ten-year world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Saturday kids, because they'll grow up with no first job to learn on. I'd want shops to keep a few people on, just so young people learn how to talk to customers. I'd vote for whoever promises that.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuse** for leaving anyone behind.
Workers need **free courses**, paid apprentices and a **say** in robot use.
think: He'll be **an engineer** for years before robots reach the shop floor in 2039.
The bigger risk is getting **comfortable** on the tills.
do: **Start** the **electrics course** one evening a week this year.
**Apply** for an apprenticeship next year and later study **robotics**.
**Save** a little every month while there's time.
feel: **Calm**, as if he is finally **the one deciding**.
S4.quote: My hard date is off the tills by thirty, and I'd tell my mum so she nags me every Sunday.
fieldNote: The decade makes him feel **in control** for the first time.
He knows his weakness is **comfort**, so he sets a deadline.
His concern for **young workers** losing first jobs stays strong.

steps.text: Start the electrics course one evening a week this year
Save a little each month toward an apprenticeship year
Vote for candidates who protect first jobs for young people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be racing everybody else for the same few servicing jobs with no savings behind me. What would help is free fast-track training and some money to live on while I do it. A loan I can't afford doesn't count.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the shop floor teaches you. I learned to calm down angry people and fix things under pressure on those tills, and nobody counts that as a skill on paper.

headlineQuote: I learned to calm down angry people and fix things under pressure on those tills, and nobody counts that as a skill on paper.
portrait: Gareth, 27, runs the **self-checkout bank** at the Valleyfresh superstore and lives alone in a studio.
He has about **two weeks** saved and a **£600** credit card to clear.
He uses AI daily and wants to become an engineer **servicing machines**.
He backs the **union** and worries most for older and very young colleagues.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, then back as time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, racing others for few **servicing jobs** with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Free **fast-track training** plus **living money** while he studies.
